Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
744 PM EDT Tue Sep 1 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 304 PM EDT Tuesday...

No significant changes were made with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 304 PM EDT Tuesday...

1. Patchy drizzle overnight gives way to more widespread 
showers later Wednesday into Thursday. Some embedded rumbles of 
thunder will be possible, along with gusty winds and locally 
heavy rainfall.

2. Scattered showers expected to end the work week. 

3. A few showers may linger into Saturday, then dry weather is 
likely into early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 304 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: This morning's showers, which brought upwards of a third 
of a inch of rain to our southern and western areas, have pushed to 
our south this afternoon. This activity was associated with a wave 
of low pressure riding along a nearly stationary frontal boundary, 
which stretches from roughly the eastern end of Lake Ontario, 
through central NY and down into southern New England. While drier 
air, evident on satellite imagery, is spreading in at mid-levels, 
low-level moisture will remain fairly abundant this evening and 
overnight, especially along the southern/eastern slopes of the 
Adirondacks and in eastern VT, where southeast flow will allow 
moisture to settle under the inversion. In these areas, expect there 
will be patchy drizzle and perhaps periods of light rain. Otherwise, 
tonight will be dry with lows in the 50s to near 60F.

More widespread precipitation is expected Wednesday and Wednesday 
night as another system rides along the aforementioned stationary 
front. This system will be more dynamic than the one that moved 
through this morning, with a surface low to trek along the St 
Lawrence Valley into southern Quebec. Shear will be ample given a 
potent 40-50 kt 850 mb jet ahead of the low, resulting in 0-6km 
shear values of 30-40 kt. The main question will be instability, 
which will likely be limited by extensive cloud cover early in the 
day. However, some clearing will be possible during the afternoon, 
particularly in northern NY, with MU CAPE values of 500-1000 J/kg. 
While some pop-up showers/thunderstorms can't be totally ruled out 
in the afternoon, expect the bulk of any activity to hold off until 
late afternoon/early evening, approaching the St Lawrence Valley 
around sunset or so. There could be enough lingering daytime 
instability to allow for more robust thunderstorms to develop, 
including the potential for small scale bowing features. Strong 
winds would be the biggest threat, restricted to just areas west of 
the Adirondacks, where the latest Day 2 Severe Weather Outlook 
continues to indicate a Marginal Risk (Level 1 out of 5) for 
strong/severe thunderstorms. 

All that said, overall expect embedded thunderstorms within a broad 
swath of moderate rain to spread from west to east Wednesday evening 
and Wednesday night. Rainfall could be heavy at times, with the HREF 
indicating localized 3-hr amounts of 1-2 inches overnight. Since 
much of our region missed out on significant rainfall today, don't 
anticipate any widespread flooding issues, but ponding of water in 
poor drainage areas will be possible. Gusty south winds will be 
possible regardless, especially here in the Champlain Valley where 
channeling will allow gusts up to 30 mph, locally higher over Lake 
Champlain into the Islands. Elsewhere, expect gusts mainly 25 mph or 
less overnight into Thursday. 

Showers quickly exit to the southeast by mid-morning Thursday, 
followed by drier air and subsidence. Scattered showers with a few 
thunderstorms will develop during the afternoon as a weak surface 
trough/frontal boundary crosses from northwest to southeast. 
However, expect most areas will only see a brief shower with perhaps 
some rumbles of thunder at worst.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Any lingering showers will end Thursday night with the 
loss of daytime heating and an influx of drier air spilling into the 
region from the north. However, we expect showers to redevelop again 
Friday afternoon as the upper trough starts to swing southward 
across eastern Quebec and into northern Maine. Showers will be 
focused over the northern high terrain, especially in northern 
Vermont, closest to the incoming trough. Otherwise, partly to mostly 
cloudy skies are expected. Highs will be seasonable, generally in 
the 70s, with northwest winds a little on the breezy side.

KEY MESSAGE 3: The upper-level low centered over central Quebec will 
shift southeastward Friday night and Saturday. Multiple shortwaves 
rotating around the low will keep some scattered showers around, 
interspersed with drier periods in between shortwaves. On Saturday, 
flow will become northeasterly and thus favor showers on the 
northeastern slopes. Sunday looks drier as the low moves out to sea 
and high pressure builds in from the west. Given the lingering upper-
level low, temperatures will remain near to cooler than seasonal 
normals. Highs throughout the weekend will generally be in the upper 
60s to mid 70s, with lows in the 40s and 50s. Beyond the weekend, 
deterministic models diverge in their solutions.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 00Z Thursday...Most terminals are currently VFR with
some periodic reductions of ceilings into the MVFR range at SLK
and RUT. Ceilings will lower as the night goes on and they will
fall to a mix of MVFR and VFR, with some intervals of IFR 
possible at MPV. While not expected, if the skies manage to 
clear out at SLK, fog formation would be possible there later in
the night. Ceilings will increase tomorrow morning and they 
should all be VFR by mid-morning. Winds will mostly be 
southerly/southeasterly tonight and under 10 KT. Winds will 
increase significantly during the day tomorrow, with southerly 
gusts in the 15-25 KT range for most areas, with gusts up to 30 
KT possible in the Champlain Valley. Scattered showers and 
thunderstorms will develop late tomorrow afternoon and continue 
into the evening. The highest probabilities of thunder and 
reduced visibility will be at SLK and MSS. 

Outlook...

Wednesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Definite
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Chance SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight
chance SHRA.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Saturday Night: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
